pages.text: At the end of Maple Street, in a little garage with a squeaky blue door, there lived a moto named Mikey. A moto, in case you haven't met one, is a motorcycle — small and quick and shiny, with exactly two wheels.

Mikey was red — the brightest red on all of Maple Street — with one white stripe. He had one round headlight, one little seat, one small horn that went meep!, and one engine that hummed like a happy bee.
"Two wheels," Mikey liked to say. "One stripe. One light. One me. Just enough of everything."

On sunny mornings, Mikey zipped down Maple Street with the wind whistling past his mirrors. He zoomed past the bakery, where the air smelled like warm bread. He took the big curve by the park, leaning way, way over — whooosh — until the whole world tilted just right.
And he always slowed down at the green house with the red door, where someone small stood at the window and waved. Meep! Meep! Mikey waved back the only way a moto can.
Vrum-vrum-zoooom! Being a moto, Mikey was quite sure, was the best thing anyone could be.
Then came the gray morning. Mikey rolled to his garage door, ready to zoom — and stopped. Pit-pat. Pit-pat-pit-pat. Rain.
Now, motos and rain do not mix. Motos have no roof to keep them dry. No wipers to swish the drops away. And rainy roads are far too slippery for leaning. So Mikey stayed inside and watched.

The cars went by all day long. Swish, swish, went their wipers. Their roofs kept them dry as toast. Their four wheels held the road, steady and sure. They splashed through puddles like it was nothing at all.
Mikey watched, and a gray feeling settled over him, gray as the sky. "They get to go everywhere," he said softly. "Rain or shine."
He watched one more car swish past his window. And that is when Mikey had his big idea. "I know," he said. "I'll just become a car."
The next morning, Mikey got to work. First: wheels. Cars had four, so Mikey found two old wagon wheels behind the garage and leaned one against each side.
He took one wobbly roll forward — Clatter! Clatter-clatter-clatter! — and both wheels tipped over and rolled away down the hill. "Wait!" called Mikey. "Come back, wheels!" They did not come back.

Next: a roof. Cars had roofs, so Mikey found a big cardboard box and wiggled underneath it. But the box slid down over his headlight, and everything went dark. "Who turned off the street?" said Mikey, from inside the box.
Then the wind came along, lifted the box right up, and carried it away like a kite with no string.
Next: the sound. Cars had big, deep, rumbly engines. Mikey took a breath and tried his very deepest voice. "RRRRUMBLE," tried Mikey. "Vreeeee!" sang his engine instead, high and happy as always.
He even tried a big car honk. "HONNNK," he tried. "Meep!" said his horn.

Last of all, Mikey rolled into a great big parking space, the kind made for great big cars, and stood very still, trying to feel wide. He did not feel wide. He felt like one small moto in one big empty square.
"Hmph," said Mikey. But he did not give up. Somehow, some day, he would be a car.

chapters.title: The Sun Came Back (But Mikey Didn't)

pages.text: The very next morning, the sun came back. It dried the roads. It warmed the street. It made the puddles small, then tiny, then gone.
The big curve by the park sat waiting, smooth and dry — a perfect day for leaning. But Mikey's garage door stayed shut.
Inside, Mikey was busy taping his cardboard box back together. "Can't stop now," he said. "What if it rains again?"
The next day was sunny too. Down the street, at the green house with the red door, someone small watched the road and wondered where the little red moto had gone.
But Mikey was hunting for sturdier wheels. "What if it rains again?" he said.
The rain was gone, you see. But Mikey's worry had stayed.
And so the sunny days went by — one, two, three — and Mikey missed every single one.
On the fourth sunny day, a car pulled up outside Mikey's garage. She was round and sky-blue, with four steady wheels, two bright headlights, and an engine that purred like a very large cat.
"¡Hola!" she called. "I'm Carla. What are you building in there?" "A car," said Mikey, from under his cardboard box. "I'm becoming a car."
Carla blinked her headlights. "Whatever for? You're a moto!" Mikey pushed the box off. "Motos can't go out in the rain," he said. "Cars can. Cars get everything."
Carla was quiet for a moment. Then she laughed — not a mean laugh, a surprised one. "That's funny," she said. "Because all my life, I've wanted to be a moto." "You — what?"
"I tried leaning once, at the big curve by the park," said Carla. "Cars can't lean. I just went around it, flat as a pancake."

"I've tried to feel the wind, but I only get a little, through a crack in my window. And that tiny parking spot under the maple tree — the shadiest, best spot on the whole street? I have never once fit."
Mikey stared. "But you have a roof! When it rains, you get to go anywhere!" "And you have the wind!" said Carla. "When it's sunny, you get to almost-fly!"
"You have four wheels. You never ever wobble." "You have two — so you get to lean. Do you know what leaning looks like from over here? It looks like dancing."

Mikey didn't know what to say. So he said the true thing, very quietly. "It rained. And I couldn't go out. And I didn't ever want to feel that way again." "Ah," said Carla gently. "It was a big rain?" "A very big rain."

"Rainy days are like that," she said. "Big and loud... and then gone." She rolled a little closer. "Days come and days go, Mikey. Sunny ones, rainy ones — none of them stay. But do you know what stays?"
"What?" said Mikey. "You. Rain or shine, you are still you. So if you turn into a car because of one rainy day... who will be the moto on all the sunny ones?"
Mikey looked past her, down Maple Street — at the dry road, the warm light, the big curve waiting by the park. Something in him went click, soft as a kickstand. "Me," he said. "I will."
Mikey rolled out of his garage, and the sun landed warm on his one white stripe. He started slow. Then a little faster. Then — Vrum-vrum-zoooom!

Down Maple Street! Past the bakery and its warm-bread smell! And there was the big curve by the park, and Mikey leaned way, way over — whooosh — and the whole world tilted just right, and the wind sang past his mirrors, and his engine went vreeeee! at the very top of its happy voice.
He slowed at the green house with the red door. The someone small was at the window — and oh, what a wave Mikey got. Both arms. The biggest wave yet. Meep! Meep!
At the corner, Carla caught up, and they stopped side by side at the light. Her engine purred, deep and steady. His engine hummed, high and bright.
Two different songs. Both of them exactly right.
"Race you to the maple tree," said Mikey. "You'll win," said Carla, smiling. "You'll fit." "Then I'll save you the shade," said Mikey — and zoom, he was off.
Some days later, the gray clouds gathered again. Pit-pat. Pit-pat-pit-pat. Rain.
But this time, Mikey knew just what to do.
He tucked himself into his little garage and watched the rain make circles in the puddles.
Because here is a thing Mikey had figured out: he didn't have a roof. But home did.
Carla parked close by, her wipers going swish, swish, slow and sleepy.
"What does rain sound like on a roof?" Mikey asked her. "Like tiny drums," said Carla.
"What does wind feel like, on the big curve?" Mikey thought about it. "Like the whole sky saying wheee."
They watched the rain together for a long, long time.
The evening came, soft and blue. The streetlights blinked on, one by one.
And Mikey did the thing motos do when the day is done: he let his engine slow down, all the way down, to the smallest, softest hum.
Hummmm in. Hummmm out.
You can hum too, if you like. In... and out... slow as a sleepy engine.
The rain grew quieter.
The clouds drifted apart, just a little, and the moon peeked through — the same moon that watches over all the motos, and all the cars, and all the small someones in green houses everywhere.
"Tomorrow might be sunny," Mikey murmured. "Or rainy. Days come, and days go..."
His engine gave one soft, sure hum. "...but I stay me."
Rain or shine, Mikey knew exactly who he would be.
Two wheels. One stripe. One light. One me. Just enough of everything.
Carla's headlights dimmed, gentle as a goodnight. "Buenas noches, Mikey."
And Mikey the moto closed his one round headlight... and hummed himself to sleep.

vocab.kidDefinition: a small, zippy bike with an engine that goes vroom
shaky and tippy, like you might fall right over
the little arms on a car that swish the rain off the window
made the soft, rumbly hum of a very happy cat
the little metal leg that holds a bike up when it rests
said something very softly, almost like a whisper
bending over to one side, the way a tree bends in the wind
